unit.title: Blamed for bad luck
unit.needIt: Two people do the same careless thing and only one is punished, because only one was unlucky. Seeing that changes how you judge others and yourself.
unit.why: Imagine two drivers who both drive home while distracted. One gets home safely, and the other hits a child. We often judge the second driver as a 'bad person' even though both made the exact same choice. This shows how our brains struggle to separate a person's choices from the luck of the outcome.
unit.outcome: Recognize how framing and luck influence your moral judgments.
unit.reachesYou: You see this when you judge a friend for a mistake that was mostly an accident. You also feel it when you see news stories where people are blamed for things they couldn't fully control.
unit.do: Think of a time you judged someone harshly. Ask yourself if they were actually in control of the final result.

quiz.q: What does Sunstein say about heuristics in moral cases?
quiz.why: Sunstein argues that heuristics are used in moral cases just as they are in non-moral cases.
quiz.quote: And then went on to contend that just as heuristics are non-moral cases, so too does it occur in moral cases.

quiz.q: How did the clicker results change when the disease case was inverted?
quiz.why: When the framing changed from 'who lives' to 'who dies', the majority opinion flipped.
quiz.quote: When we inverted the framing, the numbers came out exactly the opposite.

quiz.q: What happens in the crying baby case if you shift your attention?
quiz.why: Redirecting attention to the other people in the room changes the moral judgment.
quiz.quote: And this shiftiness in the direction of our attention is something that's going to be endemic to all of these kinds of cases.

quiz.q: Why do people resist the idea of 'cap and trade'?
choices: It feels like paying to pollute
quiz.why: People use a heuristic that says you shouldn't be able to pay your way out of wrongdoing.
quiz.quote: the heuristic attribute, people are paying to pollute, you shouldn't be able to pay your way out of serious wrongdoing, strikes us as problematic.

quiz.why: It is the idea that people should not be blamed for things beyond their control.
quiz.quote: That moral place and blame shouldn't be assigned in cases where the action or the consequences lie beyond the agent's control.

quiz.why: Resultant luck is when an action goes awry in a way the agent did not expect.
quiz.quote: That's one class of cases of moral luck. But it's harder to see how we can use that explanation for some of the deep and profound instances.

choices: Luck that affects the outcome of an action.
Luck that shapes your genes and upbringing.
Luck that affects the environment around you.
Luck that determines if you are in a war.
quiz.why: Constitutive luck refers to the features like genes and family that shape a person's character.
quiz.quote: Some of you were born with genes that make it easier for you to behave in altruistic ways, and some of you weren't.
